blocks.text: Dataset collection is the process of gathering the raw examples that will eventually become a fine-tuning dataset, whether pulled from historical records, written by hand, or generated with help from another model.

This is usually the slowest and most consequential stage in the entire fine-tuning workflow, since every downstream step, cleaning, formatting, training, and evaluation, is limited by what actually gets collected here.
1. The Three Main Sources of Training Data

blocks.alt: The Three Main Sources of Training Data
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357270-833086637.png

Most fine-tuning datasets draw from some combination of three sources, historical logs from an existing system, examples written by hand specifically for training, and synthetic examples generated with the help of another model.
Each source carries a different mix of cost, realism, and control, and later topics in this module cover the tradeoffs of each in more depth, including a dedicated topic on synthetic data generation.
2. Production Logs vs Purpose Written Examples

blocks.alt: Production Logs vs Purpose Written Examples
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357271-896648545.png

Production logs, real interactions your system already handled, tend to reflect genuine, messy, realistic input, but they may also contain mistakes, inconsistent quality, or behavior you specifically do not want the model to learn.

Purpose written examples, created deliberately to demonstrate the exact target behavior, give you more control over quality and consistency, but they cost more effort to produce and can drift away from how real users actually phrase things if written carelessly.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Source","Strength","Weakness"],"rows":[["Production logs","Realistic, reflects actual usage patterns","May contain errors or inconsistent quality"],["Purpose written examples","High control over quality and consistency","Can drift from realistic phrasing if not careful"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Starting From a Precise Task Definition

blocks.alt: Starting From a Precise Task Definition
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357272-425721450.png

Collection should not start until the task is defined precisely enough to know what a correct example actually looks like, echoing the task definition step covered in the Introduction to Fine-Tuning module.
Without that clarity, teams often end up collecting a large volume of data that turns out to be the wrong shape once the task definition finally solidifies, wasting significant effort.
4. Consent, Privacy, and Data You Are Allowed to Use

blocks.alt: Consent, Privacy, and Data You Are Allowed to Use
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357272-547956111.png

Before collecting any data that involves real user interactions, confirm you actually have the right to use it for training, whether through terms of service, explicit consent, or an internal data governance policy.
This check matters both legally and ethically, and skipping it can create serious problems well after a model has already been trained and deployed.

blocks.title: Check this before collecting, not after
blocks.content: Discovering a consent or privacy problem after training is far more costly to fix than confirming data usage rights before collection even begins.

blocks.text: 5. Diversity of Sources and Examples
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357272-936969407.png

A dataset drawn from a single narrow source, one customer segment, one time period, one writing style, risks teaching the model a narrow slice of the task rather than the full range of situations it will actually face in production.
Collecting from multiple sources, different customer types, different times, different edge cases, tends to produce a model that generalizes better once deployed.
6. Starting With a Small Pilot Collection

blocks.alt: Starting With a Small Pilot Collection
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357273-135555417.png

Rather than collecting the entire planned dataset in one pass, collecting a small pilot batch first, a few dozen to a few hundred examples, lets you validate the collection approach and catch problems early, before investing in the full volume.

code.content:
# A simple structure for tracking a collection pilot
pilot_examples = collect_examples(source="support_logs", limit=100)
review_notes = manual_review(pilot_examples)
if review_notes.quality_acceptable:
    proceed_to_full_collection()
else:
    adjust_collection_criteria(review_notes)

blocks.text: 7. Tracking Metadata While You Collect
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357273-259269304.png

Recording metadata alongside each collected example, its source, the date it was collected, and any relevant context, makes later stages, cleaning, deduplication, and debugging a trained model behavior, far easier to reason about.
Without that metadata, tracing a strange model behavior back to a specific batch or source of training data becomes close to impossible.
8. Balancing Volume Against Time and Cost

More data is not automatically better, since collection takes real time and, for purpose written or heavily reviewed examples, real cost. The right volume depends on the fine-tuning method chosen and how narrow the task is, a decision this course revisits once specific methods are covered.

A reasonable approach is collecting enough for a first solid pass, evaluating, and then collecting more, targeted at whatever gaps the evaluation reveals, rather than trying to guess the perfect volume upfront.
9. Handing Off to Cleaning and Formatting

Raw collected data is rarely training ready as is, it typically needs cleaning to remove errors and duplicates, and formatting into the specific structure a fine-tuning pipeline expects, both covered directly in the next two topics of this module.
Worked Example

A team building a fine-tuned email drafting assistant starts by collecting one thousand real emails sent by their team over the past year, tagging each with metadata including the sender, the recipient type, and the outcome of the email.

After a small pilot review, they notice the logs are heavily skewed toward one type of email, so they deliberately collect additional examples covering underrepresented categories, ending up with a more balanced and representative final collection before moving on to cleaning.
Common Mistakes

items: Beginning large scale collection before the task definition is precise enough to know what a correct example looks like
Skipping a consent or privacy check on data involving real users
Collecting from only one narrow source, producing a dataset that fails to generalize
Discarding metadata during collection, making later debugging and auditing much harder

blocks.text: Practice

For a fine-tuning task you have in mind, list every realistic source of training data available to you, logs, hand written examples, or synthetic generation, and note the strength and weakness of each source for your specific task.
Key Takeaway

Dataset collection is the foundation every later stage of fine-tuning depends on, and getting it right means starting from a precise task definition, drawing from diverse and properly consented sources, piloting before scaling up, and tracking metadata throughout so the resulting dataset is both representative and traceable.
